chapters.title: Chapter 6: Execution at Scale: Algos, Slicing, and Managing Impact

lessons.title: Order Slicing in Practice: What Retail and Prop Platforms Offer

children.text: The last lesson covered TWAP, VWAP, and POV as ideas. This lesson covers what is actually sitting on the screen in front of a real Indian trader, and the gap between a retail platform and an institutional one turns out to matter for capacity, not just convenience.
Retail Platforms: Manual Slicing and Basic Tools

A retail trader on Zerodha's Kite, or a comparable retail platform, does not get a native TWAP, VWAP, or POV order type in the interface. What is available is manual order placement, GTT (good-till-triggered) orders, and bracket or cover orders for basic risk management. A retail trader comfortable with code can go further using the Kite Connect API, writing a script that places smaller orders on a timer or checks recent volume before firing the next slice, effectively building a rough TWAP or POV by hand. SEBI has also been progressively tightening oversight of algorithmic strategies run through broker APIs, so any serious API-based execution setup today needs to account for the applicable registration and tagging requirements, not just the trading logic itself.
Institutional and Prop Desk Platforms: Built-In Execution Algos

markDefs.definition: A connection that sends orders straight to the exchange's matching engine with minimal manual intervention, typically available to institutional and prop trading accounts rather than standard retail accounts.

children.text: A prop desk or institutional trader, by contrast, typically works from an OMS or EMS, order and execution management systems, that offer TWAP, VWAP, POV, and often more advanced implementation-shortfall algorithms as selectable order types, built and maintained by the broker's institutional desk or a dedicated EMS vendor. children.text: A Uniquely Indian Point: Smart Order Routing Matters Less Here

In fragmented markets like the US, where the same stock trades across a dozen or more venues, smart order routing across exchanges is a major part of good execution. In India, NSE overwhelmingly dominates liquidity for almost every stock, with BSE a distant second for most names. Smart order routing still exists and gets used, but it is a smaller lever here than the sheer choice of algorithm, TWAP, VWAP, or POV, and the participation rate behind it.
Why This Gap Matters for Capacity

body.text: A strategy executed with basic manual or self-built API slicing can look more capacity constrained than the same strategy run through a proper institutional EMS with true POV and DMA. Better execution tooling effectively improves the calibration constant Y from Chapter 2's square-root model, meaning realized capacity is not just a function of the signal and the instrument's liquidity, it is also a function of the execution infrastructure behind it. This is one real, legitimate reason a strategy's capacity can grow simply by moving from a retail setup to a proper institutional one, with no change to the underlying logic at all.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: A prop trader can select a built-in POV algorithm directly in their firm's EMS. A retail trader on Zerodha wanting similar behavior must instead:
options: Ask Zerodha support to enable a POV order type manually
Build the logic themselves using the Kite Connect API, since native TWAP, VWAP, and POV order types are not offered on the retail platform
Use a bracket order, which behaves identically to POV
This is not achievable for any retail trader anywhere
body.explanation: Retail platforms like Kite do not natively offer TWAP, VWAP, or POV order types. A retail trader who wants that behavior has to build it themselves through the Kite Connect API, which is exactly how many independent Indian quant traders bridge the gap before moving to institutional infrastructure.

body.text: The gap between a retail platform and an institutional one is not just about convenience or speed. It is a real input into a strategy's realized capacity, since a strategy executed badly can look capacity constrained for reasons that have nothing to do with its signal or the instrument's true liquidity.

points: Retail platforms like Zerodha's Kite do not offer native TWAP, VWAP, or POV order types, leaving manual trading or self-built Kite Connect API logic as the available options.
Institutional and prop desk platforms typically offer these algorithms as built-in order types, alongside Direct Market Access and, for the fastest strategies, colocation.
Smart order routing across exchanges matters far less in India, where NSE dominates liquidity for most stocks, than it does in fragmented markets like the US.

Execution infrastructure is a genuine input into realized capacity, since better tooling effectively improves the impact-model calibration, meaning the same signal can support more capital once properly executed.
